title: The Long, Strange History of Tarot Cards: From the 14th Century to Modern Times

body:
in History |   	September 24th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

We have any num­ber of rea­sons for dif­fi­cul­ty get­ting to sleep, not least wor­ries about the future. This is hard­ly a recent phe­nom­e­non, and indeed prac­tices meant to clar­i­fy the nature of events to come may be old­er than civ­i­liza­tion itself. In fact, many of us mod­erns trust the old ways of for­tune-telling more than the new. Take the cards of the Tarot, often fea­tured here on Open Cul­ture, whose rec­og­niz­able Euro­pean form dates back to at least the four­teenth cen­tu­ry. But as explained in the new video above from YouTube chan­nel Bed­time & His­to­ri­an, their pre-his­to­ry begins longer ago and far­ther away, with the inven­tion of the play­ing card itself in Tang-Dynasty Chi­na. For Tarot decks weren’t orig­i­nal­ly a means of glimps­ing the future, but of pass­ing time in the present.
In the 400 years or so between the civ­i­liza­tion­al jour­ney play­ing cards made along the Silk Road and their first employ­ment as a div­ina­tion tool by French occultists, many a game of Tarot — or taroc­chi, Tarock, and so on — took place in Europe. Mon­e­tary stakes, and some­times con­sid­er­able ones, were not unknown, which drew the ire of both state and Church author­i­ties.
Yet not only did the cards sur­vive these attempts at repres­sion, they evolved along numer­ous long and wind­ing cul­tur­al paths, tak­ing artis­ti­cal­ly elab­o­rate and evoca­tive forms that still cap­ture the imag­i­na­tion today. At the same time, the struc­ture of the Tarot deck used by eso­teri­cists has remained remark­ably sta­ble, with its 78 cards con­sist­ing of 22 Major Arcana and 56 Minor Arcana, the lat­ter divid­ed into four suits (like the stan­dard deck used for pok­er or black­jack).
If you aren’t sure what some of those terms mean, know that all is clar­i­fied over the course of the video’s near­ly three-hour run­time, the final third of which is ded­i­cat­ed to explain­ing the iden­ti­ties, char­ac­ter­is­tics, and mean­ings of the cards them­selves. It’s worth a lis­ten as a kind of advance prepa­ra­tion if you’ve con­sid­ered going in to get a Tarot read­ing done by one of the pro­fes­sion­als who still ply their trade all around the world. (In Korea, where I live, they even work out of booths set up on the side­walk, a true con­ve­nience for com­muters in need of spir­i­tu­al guid­ance on the way home.) True to Bed­time & His­to­ri­an’s con­cept, the nar­ra­tor speaks as slow­ly and calm­ly as pos­si­ble, with a fire crack­ling in the back­ground. You’ll learn a lot about Tarot, cer­tain­ly, but you may also find that your sleep trou­bles have been solved before you’ve drawn your first card.

He’s the author of the newslet­ter Books on Cities as well as the books 한국 요약 금지 (No Sum­ma­riz­ing Korea) and Kore­an Newtro. Fol­low him on the social net­work for­mer­ly known as Twit­ter at @colinmarshall.

title: How to Memorize an Entire Chapter from “Moby Dick”:  The Art and Science of Remembering Everything
description: Some­times, when I can’t sleep, I men­tal­ly revis­it the var­i­ous homes of my child­hood, wan­der­ing from room to room, turn­ing on lights
body:
Some­times, when I can’t sleep, I men­tal­ly revis­it the var­i­ous homes of my child­hood, wan­der­ing from room to room, turn­ing on lights and peer­ing in clos­ets until I conk out.
Turns out these imag­i­nary tours are also handy mnemon­ic tools, as Vox’s Dean Peter­son explains above.
Hey, that’s good news… isn’t the sub­con­scious rumored to do some heavy lift­ing in terms of pro­cess­ing infor­ma­tion?
Peter­son con­quered a self-described bad mem­o­ry, at least tem­porar­i­ly, by traips­ing around his apart­ment, deposit­ing vivid sen­tence-by-sen­tence clues that would even­tu­al­ly help him recite by heart one of his favorite chap­ters in Moby Dick.
In truth, he was plant­i­ng these clues in his hip­pocam­pus, the rel­a­tive­ly small struc­ture in the brain that’s a crit­i­cal play­er when it comes to mem­o­ry, includ­ing the spa­tial mem­o­ries that allow us to nav­i­gate famil­iar loca­tions with­out seem­ing to give the mat­ter any thought.
What made it stick was pair­ing his every­day coor­di­nates to extra­or­di­nary visu­als.
Chap­ter 37, for those keep­ing track at home, is a mono­logue for Cap­tain Ahab in which he describes him­self as not just mad but “mad­ness mad­dened.” Here’s the first sen­tence:
I leave a white and tur­bid wake; pale waters, paler cheeks, where’er I sail.

Not the eas­i­est text for 21st-cen­tu­ry heads to wrap around, though with a lit­tle effort, most of us get the gist.
Let’s not get hung up on lit­er­ary inter­pre­ta­tion here, though, folks. Hav­ing set­tled on his front stoop as the first stop of his mem­o­ry palace Peter­son refrained from pic­tur­ing frothy spume lap­ping at the low­er­most step. Instead he plunked down a funer­al wreath and direc­tor John Waters, pale of suit and cheek, weep­ing. Get it? White? Wake? Pale cheeks?
After which Peter­son moved on to the next sen­tence.
There are 38 in all, and after sev­er­al days of prac­tice in which he men­tal­ly walked the image-strewn course of his apart­ment-cum-Mem­o­ry Palace, Peter­son was able to regale his cowork­ers with an off-book recita­tion.
The time fac­tor will def­i­nite­ly be a let­down for those hop­ing for a low-com­mit­ment par­ty trick.
Peter­son spent three-to-four hours a day pac­ing his spa­tial mem­o­ry, admir­ing the odd­i­ties he him­self had placed there.
The incred­u­lous com­ments from those ques­tion­ing the effi­cien­cy of giv­ing up half a day to mem­o­rize a page and a half are bal­anced by tes­ti­mo­ni­als from those who’ve met with suc­cess, using the Mem­o­ry Palace method to retain vast amounts of data pri­or to an exam.
That may, ulti­mate­ly, be a bet­ter use of the Mem­o­ry Palace. Peter­son gets an A for spit­ting out the lines as writ­ten, but his expres­sion is that of an actor audi­tion­ing with mate­r­i­al he has not yet mas­tered. (No shade on Peterson’s act­ing tal­ent or lack thereof—even great actors get this face when their lines are shaky. One friend doesn’t con­sid­er her­self off book until she can get all the way through her mono­logue whilst hop­ping on one foot.)
For more infor­ma­tion on build­ing a Mem­o­ry Palace, refer, as Peter­son did, to author Joshua Foer’s Moon­walk­ing With Ein­stein: The Art and Sci­ence of Remem­ber­ing Every­thing, or to his appear­ance on Adam Grant’s TED Work Life pod­cast. Stream it here:
If you would like to go whale to whale with Peter­son, below is the text that he installed in his Mem­o­ry Palace, com­pli­ments of Her­man Melville:
I leave a white and tur­bid wake; pale waters, paler cheeks, where’er I sail. The envi­ous bil­lows side­long swell to whelm my track; let them; but first I pass.
Yon­der, by ever-brim­ming goblet’s rim, the warm waves blush like wine. The gold brow plumbs the blue. The div­er sun- slow dived from noon- goes down; my soul mounts up! she wea­ries with her end­less hill. Is, then, the crown too heavy that I wear? this Iron Crown of Lom­bardy. Yet is it bright with many a gem; I the wear­er, see not its far flash­ings; but dark­ly feel that I wear that, that daz­zling­ly con­founds. ‘Tis iron- that I know- not gold. ‘Tis split, too- that I feel; the jagged edge galls me so, my brain seems to beat against the sol­id met­al; aye, steel skull, mine; the sort that needs no hel­met in the most brain-bat­ter­ing fight!
Dry heat upon my brow? Oh! time was, when as the sun­rise nobly spurred me, so the sun­set soothed. No more. This love­ly light, it lights not me; all love­li­ness is anguish to me, since I can ne’er enjoy. Gift­ed with the high per­cep­tion, I lack the low, enjoy­ing pow­er; damned, most sub­tly and most malig­nant­ly! damned in the midst of Par­adise! Good night-good night! (wav­ing his hand, he moves from the win­dow.)
‘Twas not so hard a task. I thought to find one stub­born, at the least; but my one cogged cir­cle fits into all their var­i­ous wheels, and they revolve. Or, if you will, like so many ant-hills of pow­der, they all stand before me; and I their match. Oh, hard! that to fire oth­ers, the match itself must needs be wast­ing! What I’ve dared, I’ve willed; and what I’ve willed, I’ll do! They think me mad- Star­buck does; but I’m demo­ni­ac, I am mad­ness mad­dened! That wild mad­ness that’s only calm to com­pre­hend itself! The prophe­cy was that I should be dis­mem­bered; and- Aye! I lost this leg. I now proph­esy that I will dis­mem­ber my dis­mem­ber­er. Now, then, be the prophet and the ful­filler one. That’s more than ye, ye great gods, ever were. I laugh and hoot at ye, ye crick­et-play­ers, ye pugilists, ye deaf Burkes and blind­ed Bendi­goes! I will not say as school­boys do to bul­lies- Take some one of your own size; don’t pom­mel me! No, ye’ve knocked me down, and I am up again; but ye have run and hid­den. Come forth from behind your cot­ton bags! I have no long gun to reach ye. Come, Ahab’s com­pli­ments to ye; come and see if ye can swerve me. Swerve me? ye can­not swerve me, else ye swerve your­selves! man has ye there. Swerve me? The path to my fixed pur­pose is laid with iron rails, where­on my soul is grooved to run. Over unsound­ed gorges, through the rifled hearts of moun­tains, under tor­rents’ beds, unerr­ing­ly I rush! Naught’s an obsta­cle, naught’s an angle to the iron way!
Note: An ear­li­er ver­sion of this post appeared on our site in 2019.

title: How Else Marie Pade, a Prisoner in World War II, Became Denmark’s First Female Electronic Composer
description:
in History, Music, Uncategorized |   	September 25th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Before she became a com­pos­er of elec­tron­ic music, Else Mar
body:
in History, Music, Uncategorized |   	September 25th, 2026  Leave a Comment
	
			

	

Before she became a com­pos­er of elec­tron­ic music, Else Marie Pade was a sick child lis­ten­ing to the radio. Fre­quent kid­ney inflam­ma­tions con­signed her to bed for long peri­ods of time, which would con­sti­tute nei­ther her last nor her harsh­est expe­ri­ence of con­fine­ment. She was still young when the Nazis occu­pied her home­land of Den­mark dur­ing World War II, and per­haps her youth explains her deci­sion to spit on a col­umn of march­ing Ger­man sol­diers. She escaped cap­ture that day, run­ning right into the Dan­ish Resis­tance, for which she dis­trib­uted under­ground news­pa­pers and trained in the use of explo­sives to cut off the ene­my’s tele­phone lines in the event of an Allied inva­sion. Arrest­ed by the Gestapo in 1944, she nev­er did get to exe­cute that plan, but her real ambi­tions turned out to be much larg­er.
“I screamed out loud in fear and help­less­ness in my soli­tary cell — but no one came,” Pade wrote in an essay pub­lished in The Wire. “It was then I promised myself that if I sur­vived this I would work with music for the rest of my life. And then I felt a strange calm: light, warmth and love were all around me. I was no longer alone. This was the turn­ing point in my life.” The very next day, “I start­ed scratch­ing staves on the prison wall with my garter belt fas­ten­er, and wrote out the theme that had come to me, inspired by the vision of the night.” Though infu­ri­at­ed at first, the Com­man­dant in charge told her he would “make sure that the Red Cross brought me music paper and writ­ing uten­sils so I would refrain from vio­lence and would not dirty the wall any more.”
Pade did all she could to com­pose dur­ing her time as a pris­on­er of war. After her trans­fer to the Frøslevle­jren intern­ment camp, she was reunit­ed with her piano teacher Karen Brieg, who’d brought her into the Resis­tance in the first place. “Karen wrote out Dan­ish songs for a three-part women’s choir, and I wrote schlagers — with which I want­ed to earn mon­ey for music stud­ies when we were released.” Her com­pa­tri­ots in the wom­en’s bar­racks promised to give her the oppor­tu­ni­ty to study at the Roy­al Dan­ish Acad­e­my of Music after the war’s end, which is exact­ly what she did. Though she entered the school with thoughts of becom­ing a pianist, a 1952 Dan­marks Radio broad­cast on Pierre Scha­ef­fer­’s musique con­crète per­ma­nent­ly changed the course of her artis­tic life.
Those sound col­lages turned musi­cal expe­ri­ences sent Pade back to her bouts of child­hood sick­ness, dur­ing which her chief plea­sures came from lis­ten­ing to the world around her. The result of this inspi­ra­tion was the first work of elec­tron­ic musique con­crète com­posed in Den­mark, A Day at Dyre­havs­bakken. Learn­ing from Scha­ef­fer, and lat­er from oth­er elec­tron­ic-music pio­neers like Karl­heinz Stock­hausen, Györ­gy Ligeti and Pierre Boulez, Pade devel­oped the abil­i­ty to real­ize the musi­cal worlds she’s been explor­ing in her head all along. Their aus­tere sound­scapes could hard­ly be far­ther from the sen­ti­men­tal schlager bal­lads she’d writ­ten to keep spir­its up in the bar­racks, but as you can hear in the selec­tion from 1985 to 1995 pre­sent­ed in the com­pi­la­tion above, the son­ic imag­i­na­tion that heard an ambi­ent sym­pho­ny in drip­ping sponges, whistling ket­tles, singing birds, and trot­ting hors­es remains exhil­a­rat­ing today.

title: Fantastic Plants Spring from Taehyoung Maria Jeon's Digital Illustrations
description: “I try to avoid playing it safe or going for the obvious. Instead, I look at plants from a different perspective and express them in my own way,”
body:
“I try to avoid playing it safe or going for the obvious. Instead, I look at plants from a different perspective and express them in my own way,” South Korean artist Taehyoung Maria Jeon says about a fantastical series of illustrations. “Ironically, having rules is what gives me the freedom to experiment with plant shape.”
Although she’s trained as a printmaker and continues to build compositions in layers, Jeon turns to digital methods as she reimagines the specimens cohabitating in her apartment, beginning with leaves and stems before venturing into surreal terrain. Purple veins, red outlines, and a smattering of stars appear on the imagined life forms, their vivid color palettes furthering their sense of the uncanny.

Titled Plant Series, the project “started as a personal challenge to fill a square canvas with plants, playing with shapes and composition to pack everything in as much as possible,” she says. “As the series continues, the drawings evolve and the nuances shift, but at its heart, it is always about composition, balance, colour, and shape—and hopefully sending out positive vibes, too.”
Dozens of illustrations from the series are compiled in Folium, Jeon’s first monograph from Volume. The publisher functions like Kickstarter and asks readers to back the project before printing. You can reserve your copy on Volume’s website, and find more from the artist on Instagram.

title: Woodland Creatures Inhabit an Imaginary World in Kanako Abe's Intricate Paper Cuts
description: In tender paper collages featuring woodland creatures in relief, Kanako Abe imagines dreamlike scenes reminiscent of childhood narratives and folk
body:
In tender paper collages featuring woodland creatures in relief, Kanako Abe imagines dreamlike scenes reminiscent of childhood narratives and folk tales. Giant wolves, diminutive bunnies, and curious deer wander through a Narnia-like realm that we glimpse through foliage-filled portals. In her practice, “the paper becomes a canvas for stories untold, where every cut is a deliberate step into a world where imagination and reality intertwine,” a statement says.
Paper-cutting has long been a central tenet of Abe’s practice, which she recently applied to an ambitious forthcoming book project in collaboration with young adult novelist Caryl Lewis. The Paper Girl, published by Frances Lincoln Ltd., follows the adventures of a young protagonist who folds herself into different forms in response to others’ comments and directives only to learn how to stand up for herself by summoning the power of “no.”

The Paper Girl is slated for release on October 6. Pre-order your copy on Bookshop, and if you provide proof of purchase via a form on Quarto, you’ll receive a signed bookplate by Abe. The artist is currently working toward a curatorial endeavor at Giant Robot Gallery scheduled to open in January, which will also include her work. And next April, she’ll participate in a group exhibition at Childhood’s End Gallery in Olympia, Washington. Keep an eye on updates on Instagram.

title: Three Artists and Two Writers On Surrealist Painter Remedios Varo's Influence
description: Like the Argentinian writer Samanta Schweblin, the first time I found myself in front of a painting by the Spanish-Mexican artist Remedios Varo (1
body:
Like the Argentinian writer Samanta Schweblin, the first time I found myself in front of a painting by the Spanish-Mexican artist Remedios Varo (1908-1963), I was stunned. Who was this elegant owl-figure with dainty fingers and feet? What was animating the creaturely machine at her side with tentacle-like brushes as hands? And, would I ever be able to look away?
Feeling mesmerized and awe-struck by Varo’s Surrealist visions isn’t an uncommon position to find oneself in. A new release from Louisiana Channel interviews three artists and two writers—Schweblin being one—about Varo’s influence, particularly her precise approach to alchemy and visualizing the thin veil between the physical and spiritual world. Interspersing artworks and commentary creates an insightful tapestry of a singular artist and her enduring legacy. Watch “Remedios Varo: The Painter of Magic” below, and learn more about the artist previously on Colossal.

title: Red Moons and Lightning Illuminate Sarah Lee's Uncanny Landscapes
description: Delicate waves, mysterious fissures, and diffused lightning set some of the scenes in Sarah Lee’s dreamy landscape paintings. Moons with strangely
body:
Delicate waves, mysterious fissures, and diffused lightning set some of the scenes in Sarah Lee’s dreamy landscape paintings. Moons with strangely direct beams of light and supple mountains cradled by lakes and forests are tinged with magical realism. Most of the works seen here are part of Lee’s current solo exhibition titled Deeper at Albertz Benda, in which the artist highlights different ecosystems and the nature of clarity and concealment. She often titles her works in reference to the colors she employs, such as “Emerald Sky” and “Red Meadow in Mist.”
These apparently “empty” landscapes nod to the romantic Western tradition of seascapes and broad, open expanses that pandered to a problematic colonialist mindset, such as that of Manifest Destiny. John O’Sullivan, who coined the term, wrote that Americans possessed the fundamental right to “to overspread and to possess the whole of the continent which Providence has given us…”  In Lee’s oil paintings, a gallery statement says, “the landscape pushes back.”
“Emerald Sky” (2026), oil on canvas, 56 x 52 1/4 inches
In the misty, fuzzy edges of glaciers, glowing skies, and mountain peaks, the artist imbues a nuanced sense of the uncanny. “There is a distinct feeling that more is hidden in the scene than what meets the eye: in the recesses of the water, underneath the ice, obscured by an outcropping of coral,” the gallery says. The light perhaps shines a little too brightly or a gap opens up ominously in a field of ice. “Before Dark” draws our attention to the serene surface of a lake, and what we can see is beautiful, yet one wonders if we’re witnessing the calm before the storm.
Lee harnesses the power of the unknown, examining the way nature both nourishes us and is the ultimate authority. Humans need clean water, food, and fresh air, and we rely on these things even as our collective actions cause the environment harm along with, paradoxically, ourselves. The artist’s paintings provide a kind of filter through which to see this contradiction, as the land and water are elements we fundamentally rely on but cannot control.
Deeper continues through October 10 in New York. See more on the artist’s Instagram.
